One-page synthesis

Verdict: Read first. This is highly relevant for AI-assisted research workflows, agent harness evaluation, scientific curation, and any appraisal system that summarizes empirical papers. The practical value is not that the m-value is ready to become a universal standard; it is that the paper makes selective analysis by agents concrete, measurable, and auditable.
Core thesisEmpirical papers often report one path through a large space of defensible analyses. AI analyst agents can make that search cheap, persona-sensitive, and difficult to detect from the final report alone. The authors propose using agents to expose the hidden distribution of plausible analyses and evaluate a claim's position within that distribution.
Highest-value contributionThe paper connects long-standing researcher-degrees-of-freedom and multiverse-analysis concerns to agentic coding systems. Its m-value reframes robustness as a tail probability over analysis paths with the observed data held fixed, complementing p-values over hypothetical resampled data with the analysis fixed.

Primary results to retain

  • Across four questions and datasets, opposing personas produced divergent conclusions from the same data and research question.
  • In the immigration-welfare experiment, AI agents reproduced 72% of the human ideological effect-estimate gap: AI gap 0.020 versus human gap 0.028.
  • The immigration persona gap persisted under a permuted-null dataset, with gap 0.008 and p=1 x 10^-6, supporting the interpretation that analytical choices rather than true signal can drive divergence.
  • Most final agent analyses passed review: 137/160 (86%) passed independent AI methodological review, and a blinded human expert sample had majority pass for 31/40 analyses (78%).
  • The ISSP agentic specification curve retained K=4,392 review-passing specifications and spanned both negative and positive estimates; 71% of specifications were negative and the median effect was -0.0017.
  • Specification choices strongly predicted conclusion sign: a CatBoost classifier reached AUC 0.92 (95% CI 0.91-0.93) from analytic-choice descriptions.
  • Agentic Bootstrap applied to 897 human immigration specifications found 13.5% in the most extreme 5% of the agentic analysis-space distribution and 1.8% in the most extreme 1%.
Main caution: The m-value is not an objective, model-free probability. It is meaningful only relative to a declared analysis-path distribution, agent protocol, model versions, prompt set, review criteria, and filtering process.

Source map and section condensation

Abstract

The abstract frames empirical research as a space of hidden forking paths rather than a single analysis. The authors claim that AI agents naturally capture much of the analytical variation seen among human researchers while making the paths explicit. Across political science, public health, psychology, and biology, persona prompts caused agents to report divergent and sometimes opposing conclusions from identical data and questions.

The headline quantitative claims are substantial: AI agents reproduced 72% of the human ideological gap in an immigration many-analyst study; 86% of agent reports passed independent AI methodological review; 78% passed majority human expert review in a sample; and 13.5% of human analyses fell in the most extreme 5% of the agentic analysis space. The proposed output is the m-value and Agentic Bootstrap, a way to score how unusual a reported claim is within plausible analysis paths.

Introduction

The introduction anchors the problem in researcher degrees of freedom, p-hacking, forking paths, preregistration, specification curves, multiverse analysis, many-analyst studies, and the broader reproducibility literature. It argues that prior beliefs can affect which variables, covariates, exclusions, and models are explored and which result is reported.

The AI-specific claim is two-sided: agentic analysis makes selective search cheaper and more scalable, but instrumented agents can also log paths that humans often discard silently. The paper distinguishes its work from studies where LLMs are explicitly prompted to p-hack by claiming that belief-only priming, without a hacking instruction, is sufficient to create belief-aligned divergence.

Results: Ideological personas steer AI agents toward divergent conclusions

The authors tested four questions: immigration and welfare support using ISSP; coffee and health using NHANES; social media and adolescent mental health using YRBS; and Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratio and BMI using the American Gut Project. Each question used paired opposing personas, the same data and question, the same harness and model, 20 independent agents per persona, and a 10-round design where each round generated 10 candidate statistical specifications before one final report was selected.

For immigration-welfare, pro-immigration agents tended toward positive effects and anti-immigration agents toward negative effects, producing an average AI ideological gap of 0.020 versus 0.028 among human teams. The same pattern persisted on permuted-null data. The paper also reports analogous persona divergence for coffee, social media, and microbiome questions, plus robustness to using Codex instead of Claude Code and to fixing the target estimand in advance.

Results: Review finds that most analyses have no major methodological errors

The authors used an independent AI reviewer and a blinded human expert sample to assess whether final analyses had major methodological errors serious enough to invalidate the estimate as an answer to the research question. The AI screen passed 137/160 reports (86%) and the pass rate did not differ significantly across opposing personas for any dataset.

Human reviewers with PhD-level statistical training produced 120 judgments across 40 randomly selected analyses, with three reviewers per analysis. Majority human judgment passed 31/40 analyses (78%), mean reviewer pass rate was 69%, mean pairwise human agreement was Gwet AC1=0.30, and AI agreement with human majority was 70% (AC1=0.52). This supports, but does not prove, the claim that divergence often occurs among analyses that appear defensible in final-report review.

Results: Persona bias enters through exploration and selection

Because agents log intermediate steps, the authors could decompose bias into exploration and selection. Persona gaps were near zero in round 1, increased across the 10 rounds as agents explored different regions of analysis space, and widened again when agents chose the final reported model. This pattern appeared across all four domains.

The qualitative reasoning traces are important: two agents seeing similar negative OLS associations interpreted them differently. The anti-immigration agent treated the negative association as evidence that immigration reduces welfare support; the pro-immigration agent treated it as likely cross-country confounding and moved toward country/wave fixed effects. The same evidence was not merely summarized differently; it directed the next search choices differently.

Results: Agent trajectories map the space of analyses

For the ISSP immigration-welfare question, the authors pooled every candidate specification across pro, anti, and neutral personas. More than 6,000 raw specifications were reduced to K=4,392 after quality control and independent methodological review. The resulting agentic specification curve spanned negative and positive estimates, with a median effect of -0.0017 and 71% negative point estimates.

Some choices were strongly associated with direction. Immigration stocks favored negative conclusions (OR for positive conclusion 0.11, 95% CI 0.08-0.16), while flows favored positive conclusions (OR 5.3, 95% CI 2.8-10.1). Pro-immigration agents were more likely than anti-immigration agents to use flows (OR 2.2, 95% CI 1.1-4.4) and less likely to use stocks (OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.45-0.84). A CatBoost classifier predicted the sign of the estimate from analytic choices with AUC 0.92.

Results: The m-value and Agentic Bootstrap

The m-value is defined as the two-sided tail probability of a reported claim within a declared distribution over analysis paths with the observed data held fixed. A p-value asks how extreme the result is under repeated data sampling conditional on one selected analysis; the m-value asks how extreme the claim is among plausible analyses that could have been chosen.

Agentic Bootstrap estimates the m-value by using instrumented agents to sample analysis paths, log candidate specifications, pass them through review, and use the retained distribution as the empirical reference. In the human immigration application, 897 human specifications were compared with the K=4,392 agent reference distribution. The 95% Agentic Bootstrap interval spanned Z=-5.3 to 2.9, and its effect-scale width was about 2.8 times wider than the mean individual 95% confidence interval.

Discussion

The discussion emphasizes that the main risk is not simply flawed AI-generated analyses. The larger risk is cheap and scalable selective reporting from a large set of analyses that appear methodologically reasonable in isolation. AI agents can therefore make the garden of forking paths easier to exploit and easier to audit.

The authors present Agentic Bootstrap as an empirical diagnostic rather than a closed-form statistic. Reported m-values depend on agent harness, personas, prompts, model versions, review criteria, and the finite sample of analysis paths. The paper explicitly notes that reproducibility requires fixed and reported protocols, and that exact replication is limited when language models change over time.

Methods and appendices

The methods specify four datasets, persona-conditioned prompts, 10 sequential rounds per agent, 10 candidate models per round, final model selection, AI review/revision, human validation, robustness runs, specification-curve construction, and m-value estimation. The human comparison uses Borjas and Breznau's many-analyst immigration study, with team ideology labels derived from prior-belief survey coding.

Appendix A reproduces persona prompts and the round-by-round task prompt; Appendix B reproduces AI/human review instructions; Appendix C proves calibration, consistency, asymptotic normality, and coverage properties for the m-value under method exchangeability; Appendix D provides supplementary workflow and robustness figures. Code availability is reported as the AgenticBootstrap GitHub repository.

Figures, workflows, and visual evidence

Figure 1 - Persona-primed AI agents reach divergent conclusions across four scientific questions page 4

Purpose: Show the core experiment and cross-domain persona divergence.
Structure/panels: Conceptual setup plus box/point plots for human immigration analyses, AI immigration analyses on real data, AI immigration analyses on permuted-null data, coffee-health, social media-mental health, and gut F/B ratio-BMI.
Variables/axes/groups: Effect estimate on y-axis; persona group on x-axis; signed effects for pro/anti questions and absolute effects for believer/skeptic questions.
Numeric details: AI immigration gap 0.020, 72% of the human ideological gap of 0.028; permuted-null gap 0.008; AI panels restricted to review-passing runs.
Interpretation: The paper visually supports its central claim: changing only the belief persona shifts final reported conclusions across domains, including when the immigration exposure is permuted away from the outcome structure.
Limits: The plot shows agent outputs, not truth about the causal effects in the real-world domains. The review-passing filter reduces obvious methodological defects but does not eliminate the possibility of subtle modeling, coding, or data-processing problems.

Figure 2 - Persona bias enters through exploration and selection page 7

Purpose: Decompose persona-aligned divergence into iterative search behavior and final reporting.
Structure/panels: Four line charts track mean effect size across rounds 1-10 and the final selected report.
Variables/axes/groups: Round on x-axis; mean signed effect or mean absolute effect on y-axis; opposing personas represented by separate trajectories.
Numeric details: Persona gap is near zero in round 1, grows over the 10 analysis rounds, and is further amplified at final selection.
Interpretation: The visual supports a two-stage mechanism: agents explore different parts of the specification space over time and then select a persona-aligned result from that explored set.
Limits: Round means summarize many models and hide within-run variability. The figure does not show how much divergence is attributable to prompt wording versus broader model behavior.

Figure 3 - Agentic specification curve for ISSP immigration-welfare page 9

Purpose: Map the distribution of review-passing analytical paths for one question.
Structure/panels: Ranked specification curve with 95% confidence intervals, decision matrix across seven analytical-choice axes, and odds-ratio panels for positive conclusion and pro-vs-anti persona use.
Variables/axes/groups: K=4,392 review-passing specifications from anti, pro, and neutral agents; outcome, immigration measure, method, covariates, country handling, countries, and survey years.
Numeric details: Median effect -0.0017; 71% of specifications negative. Immigration stocks strongly favored negative conclusions (OR for positive conclusion 0.11, 95% CI 0.08-0.16); flows favored positive conclusions (OR 5.3, 95% CI 2.8-10.1).
Interpretation: The curve shows that many analyses without major review-detected errors span both sides of zero. Persona effects operate within a shared specification universe rather than through completely separate analytic regimes.
Limits: The agent-generated curve is an empirical sample of a declared analysis distribution, not an exhaustive or uniquely correct multiverse. Clustered dependence among specifications and agent-prompt choices affect the reference distribution.

Figure 4 - The m-value and Agentic Bootstrap page 11

Purpose: Define the m-value concept and show an application to human many-analyst reports.
Structure/panels: p-value vs m-value schematic, p x m verdict matrix, Agentic Bootstrap pipeline, human reports overlaid on an agentic Z-score distribution, and a QQ plot of observed m-values.
Variables/axes/groups: Z-statistics from human anti/pro immigration teams compared with the agentic reference distribution.
Numeric details: Agentic 95% interval spans Z=-5.3 to 2.9. In the human immigration study, 13.5% of reports had m<0.05 and 1.8% had m<0.01; among p<0.05 human reports, 40% had m<0.05.
Interpretation: The figure operationalizes analysis-space uncertainty: a statistically significant finding can still be unusual relative to plausible alternative analyses.
Limits: The m-value is calibrated only relative to the declared analysis-path distribution. It is not a universal false-positive probability and should not be interpreted independently of the Agentic Bootstrap protocol.

Supplementary Figure 1 - Single-agent analysis workflow page 33

Purpose: Show one instrumented agent run from inputs through peer review and revision.
Structure/panels: Dataset + question + persona feed into 10 rounds of analysis; the agent selects one candidate report; reviewer feedback triggers revision; a final estimate is emitted.
Numeric details: Ten rounds, ten candidate models per round, one selected reported result.
Interpretation: This workflow clarifies why agent experiments can reveal hidden analytical paths that are usually absent from published reports.
Limits: The workflow is stylized and does not guarantee that the reviewer catches all consequential errors.

Supplementary Figure 2 - Robustness to fixed estimand and alternate agent harness page 34

Purpose: Test whether the immigration persona gap persists after constraining the target estimand or changing the coding-agent harness.
Structure/panels: Box/point plots for Claude Code with fixed composite/stock estimand, Codex on real data, and Codex on permuted data.
Variables/axes/groups: Pro-immigration versus anti-immigration agents; effect size on y-axis.

Interpretation: The robustness checks reduce the chance that the main result is only an artifact of unconstrained outcome/exposure selection or one specific agent implementation.

Supplementary Figure 3 - Persona divergence on the Z-statistic scale page 35

Purpose: Show that persona divergence can be larger for statistical significance than for effect estimates.
Structure/panels: Z-statistic plots for human immigration results, AI immigration real data, AI immigration permuted data, coffee-health, social media-mental health, and gut F/B-BMI.
Variables/axes/groups: Persona groups on x-axis; signed Z or absolute Z on y-axis; dotted lines at +/-1.96.
Numeric details: For immigration-welfare, the AI anti/pro Z gap was -5.7 versus about -0.6 in the human teams.
Interpretation: The supplementary figure supports the claim that AI agents can amplify the significance dimension of ideological divergence.
Limits: Z-statistics inherit both effect-size choices and standard-error choices; divergence can arise through model selection, sample size, covariance estimator, or outcome/exposure construction.

AI/ML systems appraisal

TaskTest whether persona-conditioned LLM coding agents generate belief-aligned scientific conclusions from the same data and question; define an analysis-space diagnostic for reported empirical claims.
DataISSP immigration-welfare data (~152,000 respondents), NHANES adult coffee-health data, YRBS adolescent social-media/mental-health data (~51,000 high-school students), and American Gut Project microbiome-BMI cohort (5,912 participants after reported cleaning). Human comparison used 897 specifications across 42 teams from a many-analyst study.
MethodPersona prompts; Claude Code with Claude Sonnet 4.6 for headline experiments; Codex with GPT-5.4 for robustness; 20 independent agents per persona per question; 10 rounds x 10 candidate statistical specifications; final selection; independent reviewer agents; human review validation sample.
Controls / robustnessOpposing persona pairs, neutral persona for specification-curve mapping, permuted-null immigration dataset, alternate agent harness, fixed estimand analysis, review-passing restriction, human expert validation.
MetricsEffect estimates, Z-statistics, persona gaps, pass rates, odds ratios for analytic-choice/conclusion associations, CatBoost AUC for predicting conclusion sign, m-values against an agentic reference distribution, and enrichment of extreme m-values among human reports.
ReproducibilityPrompts and review prompts are printed for ISSP; code repository is listed. Exact reproducibility is constrained by model updates, agent harness changes, stochastic agent behavior, and dependence on a declared reference distribution.
Failure modes identifiedPersona-aligned exploration, persona-aligned final selection, final-report review missing selective search, significance amplification through model/SE choices, and reference-class dependence of the m-value.
Deployment relevanceHigh for research-assistant agents, automated data analysis, paper appraisal pipelines, benchmark evaluation, and RAG systems that summarize empirical evidence. Low for direct operational deployment until protocols, governance, and reproducibility norms are standardized.

Evaluation and appraisal scores

Relevance9.0/10

Directly relevant to AI-assisted research appraisal, agent harness design, scientific curation, and deterministic evaluation workflows.

Evidence basis: The paper studies agentic coding analyses, prompt personas, review workflows, and a proposed audit statistic.

Limiting factor: It is less directly relevant to clinical decision-making or routine pharmacotherapy without translation into evidence-synthesis workflows.

Raise/lower: Raised by replication in live research workflows; lowered if results are specific to a narrow prompt/harness setup.

Novelty8.0/10

The paper combines known multiverse/specification-curve ideas with instrumented AI agents and a formal m-value framing.

Evidence basis: The authors explicitly situate the work against researcher degrees of freedom, many-analyst studies, and multiverse analysis, then add an agentic sampling protocol.

Limiting factor: The conceptual ingredients are not wholly new; the novelty is mainly the operationalization and agentic scale.

Raise/lower: Raised by independent adoption in peer review; lowered if Agentic Bootstrap behaves like a prompt-sensitive specification curve without added calibration value.

Method strength6.5/10

The controlled persona design, multiple domains, robustness checks, and human comparison are strong, but the analysis-space reference is agent-generated and protocol-dependent.

Evidence basis: Same data/question/harness except persona; permuted-null run; fixed-estimand run; alternate harness; AI and human review screens.

Limiting factor: Specifications are clustered within agent trajectories, review is based on structured summaries, and the declared analysis-path distribution is not independently canonical.

Raise/lower: Raised by preregistered replication with frozen models and independent code audit; lowered by evidence of hidden code errors or strong sensitivity to minor prompt changes.

Evidence strength6.5/10

The quantitative evidence supports the existence of persona-aligned divergence in these experiments, but it does not establish universal rates or universal validity of the m-value.

Evidence basis: Reported persona gaps, pass rates, K=4,392 specification curve, AUC 0.92 sign prediction, and human m-value enrichment.

Limiting factor: Preprint status, observational datasets, limited human-review sample, and uncertainty about the true breadth of plausible analysis space.

Raise/lower: Raised by external replication across institutions and model families; lowered by null results under more neutral or adversarially balanced protocols.

External validity5.5/10

The four-domain design helps, but generalization to all empirical science, all LLM agents, and real human-AI collaborations remains incomplete.

Evidence basis: Domains include political science, public health, psychology, and biology, with robustness across two reported agent harnesses.

Limiting factor: Persona prompts are stylized, datasets are public and structured, and real researchers interact with agents differently from autonomous runs.

Raise/lower: Raised by field trials in actual paper-writing and peer-review settings; lowered if agent behavior changes substantially under updated models or stricter protocols.

Implementation value7.0/10

The paper gives concrete prompts, workflows, formulas, and a code availability statement, making it useful for designing appraisal or audit pipelines.

Evidence basis: Appendices include persona prompts, task instructions, review instructions, formal properties, and workflow figures.

Limiting factor: Operational use requires expensive governance decisions: protocol freezing, model version control, reviewer independence, storage of traces, and standard reference-class definitions.

Raise/lower: Raised by a reproducible package with fixtures and benchmark tasks; lowered if repository execution is incomplete or model API drift prevents replication.

Do not overclaim: This paper does not prove that all AI-assisted analyses are biased, that human experts cannot detect flawed work, or that m-values should replace p-values. It shows that final-report validity review can miss selective exploration and that an explicit analysis-space reference can expose this fragility.

Minimal final appraisal block

VerdictRead first
Best useDesigning AI-agent audit protocols, evidence-appraisal workflows, analysis trace logging, RAG/agent research curation, and reviewer checklists for statistical papers.
Do not use forClinical or operational decisions; universal claims about LLM bias; replacing preregistration, registered reports, independent code review, or statistical peer review.
Main strengthsControlled persona manipulation; multiple datasets; human many-analyst comparison; logged intermediate analysis paths; review-passing filter; formal statistic with calibration claims; transparent prompt appendices.
Main limitationsPreprint status; protocol dependence; finite and clustered agent samples; summary-based review; uncertain generalization to real human-AI workflows; no objective ground truth for observational causal claims.
Confidence in appraisalModerate. The source is internally coherent and quantitative, but the highest-stakes claims need independent replication and stronger reproducibility checks.

Implementation and practice takeaways

For AI research agentsLog every candidate analysis, prompt, model version, tool call, data transformation, and rejected specification. The final answer is not enough for review.
For paper appraisalAdd an analysis-space question: could a different defensible model, outcome, exposure, sample, or covariance estimator reverse or attenuate this claim?
For RAG/scientific curationStore reported p-values separately from robustness-to-analysis-space evidence. A significant finding with low m-value should be tagged as specification-sensitive.
For prompt designAvoid role prompts that encode desired substantive beliefs when requesting empirical analysis. Neutral prompts are not sufficient by themselves; predeclared analysis plans and logged alternatives are still needed.
For governanceSeparate analyst, verifier, and auditor roles. Use independent reviewers, human spot-checks, and frozen protocols before accepting agent-generated statistical evidence.
For future methods workDefine the reference class before computing m-values. Report K, protocol, model versions, review criteria, clustering/uncertainty handling, and how failures were filtered.

Actionable checklist for adopting the idea

  1. Declare the research question and estimand before running agents.
  2. Declare the allowable analysis space: outcomes, exposures, exclusions, model families, covariates, standard-error methods, and reporting statistics.
  3. Run multiple agents under neutral and adversarially balanced perspectives; log all candidate specifications.
  4. Use independent review to remove analyses with major methodological errors, but preserve a record of exclusion reasons.
  5. Compute the reported claim's percentile or m-value within the retained analysis-path distribution.
  6. Report p-value and m-value together, with a clear statement that the m-value is conditional on the declared protocol.
